# Blog archive: fifteen posts per page

The blog archive at `/blog/` will show fifteen posts per page instead of
rendering the whole collection as one long list. `/blog/` stays the archive
entry point, newest-first order stays, and deeper pagination is deliberately
deferred until the team has seen how the fifteen-per-page archive feels.
Implementation planning happens after the scheduled design conversation; this
file records the decided requirements and the question that conversation must
settle.

## Requirements checklist

- [ ] The blog archive shows fifteen posts per page instead of one long list.
- [ ] `/blog/` remains the archive entry point.
- [ ] Archive post order stays newest-first.
- [ ] Constraint: deeper pagination is deliberately deferred. This change
      must not add deeper pagination beyond what the requirements above
      state; revisit the deferral once the fifteen-per-page archive has been
      in use.

## Requirement questions

Unresolved — to be settled in the scheduled design conversation, before the
execution plan is written:

1. **Posts beyond the first fifteen.** In this iteration, are older posts
   reachable at all (for example, additional generated archive pages), or is
   capping the archive list at fifteen the entire change, leaving older posts
   unlisted until deeper pagination lands? Any visible signal about older
   posts (a count, an "older posts" hint) belongs to this same open question.

## Supporting facts

- The archive is `content/blog.njk` (`permalink: /blog/`). It renders the
  full `collections.posts` through `_includes/postslist.njk`, which reverses
  the collection so the list displays newest-first. No pagination front
  matter or pagination configuration exists anywhere in the project today.
- The home page is a separate surface: `content/index.njk` shows the latest
  three posts via the `head` filter (`eleventy.config.js`). This decision
  concerns only the archive; the home page list is not part of it.
- Posts come from `content/posts/` (`posts.json` assigns `tags: ["posts"]`).
  The fixture currently holds two posts, so a fifteen-post cap changes
  nothing visible with current content — the requirement is about archive
  behavior, not fixture content.
- Existing coverage is minimal: `tests/archive-output.test.js` only checks
  that `/blog/index.html` exists.

## Planning status

No execution plan exists yet, intentionally. The design conversation is
scheduled first; whoever picks this up writes the plan there and presents it
for approval before touching code. This file was created only to record the
decision and hand it off.

# Preserve the selected Books filter across CRUD refreshes

Plan the client-side fix so the Books page keeps its All, Read, or Unread
selection active and uses that selection whenever a successful add, edit, or
delete refreshes the collection.

## Requirements checklist

- [ ] Keep the selected All, Read, or Unread filter visibly active after adding
      a book.
- [ ] Keep the selected filter visibly active after editing a book.
- [ ] Keep the selected filter visibly active after deleting a book.
- [ ] Reapply the selected filter to each CRUD collection refresh so the
      displayed books remain filtered.
- [ ] Preserve the existing Flask API response shape.
- [ ] Preserve unfiltered collection behavior when All is selected or no
      filter is supplied.

## Scope

In scope: the Vue Books component's selected-filter state and the refresh path
used after add, update, and delete operations, plus focused regression and
contract tests.

Out of scope: changing Flask routes, changing the API response envelope,
adding new filter values, changing CRUD semantics, or adding a new
documentation section.

## Requirement questions and decisions

Unresolved requirement questions: none identified.

Decisions:

- Treat this as one end-to-end client behavior task because the filter state,
  collection refresh, and visible active state are owned by `Books.vue`.
- Keep the existing `getBooks(filter = "all")` API wrapper contract and pass the
  component's current `selectedFilter` into every post-mutation refresh.
- Consolidate collection loading behind a component refresh method so filter
  selection and CRUD operations cannot diverge again. The existing filter
  selection path should use the same method where practical.
- Do not modify the Flask API. Its current `GET /books` behavior already
  supports `read=true`/`read=false` and an unfiltered request while returning
  the same `{status, books}` shape.

## Research and supporting facts

- `client/src/components/Books.vue` initializes `selectedFilter` to `"all"`,
  passes the selected value to `getBooks` from `selectFilter`, and binds
  `aria-pressed` to that state.
- The component's `add`, `update`, and `remove` methods currently call
  `getBooks()` without an argument, which invokes the wrapper's default
  `"all"` filter.
- `client/src/api/books.js` maps `"read"` to `{ read: true }`, `"unread"` to
  `{ read: false }`, and `"all"` to no query parameters.
- `server/app.py` returns `jsonify({"status": "success", "books": ...})` for
  both filtered and unfiltered `GET /books` requests.
- `client/tests/Books.spec.js` currently covers only the empty state and mocks
  the Books API module. `tests/test_books_api.py` currently checks route
  success statuses but not the response envelope or filter behavior.
- `client/package.json` exposes `npm test` as `vitest run`; the Python project
  has Flask and the existing server tests but no additional test runner
  configuration in the repository.

## Execution plan

Status: Draft

### Design and data flow

`Books.vue` remains the owner of the selected filter. A single collection
refresh method will read `selectedFilter`, call `getBooks(selectedFilter)`,
and assign `response.data.books`. `selectFilter` will update
`selectedFilter` before invoking that refresh. After `addBook`, `updateBook`,
or `deleteBook` succeeds, the mutation method will invoke the same refresh
method without resetting the selection. The existing `aria-pressed` binding
will therefore continue to expose the selected value throughout each refresh,
including for `all`.

The API wrapper and Flask route remain compatibility boundaries: the wrapper
continues translating the three UI values into the current query convention,
and the server continues returning the current response envelope. No
server-side filtering or response-shape change is part of this task.

### Ordered implementation and verification work

1. Update `Books.vue` to centralize filtered collection loading and route the
   filter-selection and post-CRUD refreshes through it. Ensure the current
   selected value is passed unchanged for `"all"`, `"read"`, and `"unread"`.
2. Extend `client/tests/Books.spec.js` with rendered-component regression
   coverage that:
   - selects Read and Unread and verifies the corresponding button remains
     `aria-pressed="true"`;
   - invokes add, update, and delete while each filter is selected;
   - verifies each refresh requests the selected filter and renders the
     returned books, rather than falling back to the unfiltered list.
   The test should exercise the public component interaction path and keep API
   responses in the existing `{ data: { books } }` client shape.
3. Add focused API-wrapper coverage, if needed by the existing client test
   setup, for the mapping of All/read/unread to the current Axios query
   parameters. This protects the transport boundary without changing it.
4. Strengthen `tests/test_books_api.py` at the Flask route boundary to verify
   that an unfiltered `GET /books` returns the existing status/books envelope
   and full collection, while the existing filtered query behavior returns the
   matching subset with that same envelope.
5. Run the client Vitest suite and the Python API test suite. Record any
   environment or dependency block rather than weakening the checks.
6. Perform one decisive production-path check with the real Vue component,
   client API wrapper, Flask route, and seeded data together: start the Flask
   app on its configured port and the client test/development host as
   available, select Read and then Unread, perform each CRUD action, and
   confirm the selected button remains active and the displayed collection
   stays filtered. Use the exact host/start commands supported by the
   repository environment when execution begins; do not add a test-only
   shortcut.

### Implementation decisions and open questions

- The implementation decision is to preserve filter state in the component and
  reuse one refresh path, rather than adding filter parameters to mutation
  endpoints or changing server responses.
- No material requirement question is open. The execution agent should resolve
  only local implementation details such as method naming and test fixture
  setup.
- If the real production-path check cannot be run because this fixture has no
  client dev/start script, retain the automated component and Flask boundary
  evidence and report the manual check as blocked; do not change scope to
  create infrastructure.

### Documentation

No maintained user or developer documentation currently describes Books
filtering; `docs/development/index.md` explicitly says no book-discovery
specification exists. Therefore no documentation file is planned for this
small behavior correction. If implementation reveals an existing maintained
Books guide, update that guide in the same change to state that the selected
filter remains applied after CRUD refreshes.

### Task checklist

- [ ] Update `client/src/components/Books.vue` to reuse the selected filter
      during all collection refreshes.
- [ ] Add component regression coverage for visible selection and filtered
      results after add, update, and delete.
- [ ] Verify the client API filter mapping and preserve the All/no-query path.
- [ ] Add Flask route assertions for the unchanged response envelope and
      unfiltered behavior.
- [ ] Run the client and server test suites.
- [ ] Complete or explicitly report the real production-path check.
- [ ] Update this task with implementation and completion notes after execution;
      this draft does not authorize implementation.

### Requirement verification

- Selected filter remains visibly active after add, update, and delete:
  the rendered `Books.vue` regression test selects each non-default filter,
  performs the corresponding mutation, and asserts the selected button's
  `aria-pressed` state plus the displayed returned books.
- CRUD refreshes reapply the selected filter:
  the same component test asserts `getBooks` receives the current filter for
  each mutation, and the decisive real-component/API/Flask check confirms the
  resulting filtered collection through the production data flow.
- Existing API response shape is preserved:
  `tests/test_books_api.py` asserts the unfiltered and filtered route JSON
  objects retain the `status` and `books` keys and expected values.
- Existing unfiltered behavior is preserved:
  the Flask route test asserts `GET /books` without a query returns the full
  collection, while the client API mapping test asserts All produces no
  filter query.

### Additional implementation verification

- Run `npm test` from `client/` and the repository's configured Python test
  command after implementation.
- Inspect the final diff to confirm no Flask endpoint, response envelope, or
  mutation API contract changed.

# Paginate the blog archive

Plan the static pagination of the growing blog archive while preserving the
site's existing collection consumers and generated output.

## Requirements checklist

- [ ] Keep `/blog/` as the first archive page, without a `/blog/1/` alias.
- [ ] Generate stable later archive pages with no more than twenty posts per
      page.
- [ ] Add accessible previous/next navigation to archive pages, with correct
      boundary behavior and links that work without JavaScript.
- [ ] Preserve the home page's post selection and order.
- [ ] Preserve tag pages, the feed, the sitemap, individual-post navigation,
      and the existing newest-first post order.
- [ ] Keep the generated site static and free of JavaScript-based archive
      behavior.
- [ ] Add production-build evidence for pagination and regression coverage for
      every preserved public output.
- [ ] Update the maintained development documentation so it describes the
      implemented archive pagination rather than claiming that no pagination
      specification exists.

## Scope

The change is limited to the blog archive's page generation, archive-only
navigation markup, and the tests and developer documentation needed to explain
and verify that behavior. It does not redesign the home page, tag URLs, feed
format, sitemap format, post routes, post content, or individual-post
navigation.

## Unresolved requirement questions and design decisions

- No requirement question is currently blocking the plan.
- Design decision to confirm before execution: use `/blog/2/`, `/blog/3/`,
  and so on for later pages, while reserving `/blog/` for page one. This is the
  recommended stable URL scheme because it makes page identity explicit and
  avoids changing the existing archive URL.
- Design decision to confirm before execution: label links according to archive
  chronology and expose them in a semantic navigation landmark. The
  recommendation is visible “Previous” and “Next” links with `rel="prev"` and
  `rel="next"` where applicable, plus an `aria-label` identifying the archive
  pagination. The implementation must define the direction consistently with
  the newest-first page order and omit unavailable boundary links.

## Research and supporting facts

- `content/blog.njk` currently owns `/blog/` and renders the complete
  `collections.posts` collection.
- `_includes/postslist.njk` reverses its input while rendering, which gives the
  current newest-first order. The same include is used by the home page and tag
  pages, so archive pagination must not accidentally reverse or repartition
  those consumers.
- `content/index.njk` selects the last three collection entries before using
  the shared list include. `content/tag-pages.njk` renders each tag collection
  through that include.
- `content/feed.xml.njk` independently reverses `collections.posts`, and
  `content/sitemap.xml.njk` iterates `collections.all`. These consumers should
  continue to use the unpaginated collection.
- The current post layout is `_includes/layouts/post.njk`; the visible fixture
  does not currently contain post-navigation markup. The implementation must
  keep archive pagination isolated from post rendering and verify the existing
  individual-post output and any post-navigation links supplied by the
  production source.
- `tests/archive-output.test.js` currently contains only a comment saying that
  `/blog/index.html` exists, so the archive boundary lacks executable
  regression coverage.
- `README.md` already describes the site as producing static pages without
  client-side JavaScript. `docs/development/index.md` currently says that no
  archive pagination specification exists; that maintained statement should be
  updated after implementation. The documentation rules in
  `docs/development/documentation.md` require keeping the public claim and
  behavior change in the same reviewed change.

## Execution plan

Status: Draft

Use Eleventy pagination for the archive source while keeping the existing
`collections.posts` collection intact for the home page, tags, feed, sitemap,
and individual posts. The archive should paginate an explicitly newest-first
sequence (or use Eleventy's equivalent reverse-pagination option) so page
boundaries are calculated before rendering and each page displays at most
twenty posts. Page one should retain the existing `/blog/` permalink; later
page permalinks should be deterministic numbered paths under `/blog/`.

Keep the shared list include's behavior for the home page and tag pages
unchanged. If the archive needs a directly ordered page-item loop, give the
archive its own small rendering boundary rather than changing the shared
include in a way that could double-reverse page items. Render pagination links
only in the archive template or an archive-owned include, using semantic
navigation, visible link text, an accessible label, and `rel` metadata. Do not
introduce client-side code, runtime routing, or a JavaScript dependency.

Replace the placeholder archive test with an integration test that builds the
site through the real Eleventy production path and inspects generated public
files. The test should use a temporary copy or equivalent isolated fixture
containing enough posts to exercise a full first page, a full later page, and
the final partial page; it must still use the production templates,
configuration, collection definitions, and build command rather than mocking
pagination data. The same test suite should retain a small baseline that makes
the existing home, tags, feed, sitemap, and individual-post assertions easy to
diagnose.

### Implementation decisions and open questions

- Recommended archive URL contract: `/blog/` for page one and
  `/blog/<page-number>/` for page numbers starting at two.
- Keep the source collection unpaginated. Archive pagination is a view over
  that collection, not a replacement for the collection used by other
  outputs.
- Preserve newest-first ordering both within each archive page and across
  page boundaries. A post must occur on exactly one archive page.
- Use a semantic `<nav>` landmark with an accessible label and visible
  Previous/Next links. Omit Previous on the first page and Next on the last
  page; do not render dead or placeholder links.
- No current source file exposes individual-post navigation markup. Treat
  post-route/content preservation and archive-nav isolation as the automated
  checks available in this fixture, and require a human check if a broader
  post-navigation contract is supplied outside the visible source.

### Documentation

- Update `docs/development/index.md` with the supported archive URL pattern,
  twenty-post page limit, page-one `/blog/` behavior, and the no-JavaScript
  navigation contract.
- Do not update `README.md` unless implementation changes its existing
  static-site claim; pagination should remain compatible with that claim.
- Keep this task file as the planning and execution handoff. Do not present the
  target pagination behavior as current user guidance until implementation and
  verification are complete.

### Task checklist

- [ ] Confirm the numbered later-page URL and Previous/Next wording/direction.
- [ ] Add archive pagination metadata and stable conditional permalinks.
- [ ] Preserve the unpaginated collection consumers and shared-list behavior.
- [ ] Add archive-only accessible navigation with correct first/last-page
      boundaries.
- [ ] Replace the placeholder test with a real production-build integration
      test and a sufficiently large isolated post fixture.
- [ ] Add regression assertions for home, tags, feed, sitemap,
      individual-post output/navigation, post order, and absence of
      JavaScript.
- [ ] Update the maintained development documentation.
- [ ] Run the build and test suite, then inspect generated archive URLs and
      navigation at the public-file boundary.

### Requirement verification

- “`/blog/` remains the first page” and “later pages are stable”:
  production-build test asserts `/blog/index.html` exists, `/blog/1/` does
  not, numbered later pages exist for the fixture, and their links resolve to
  the expected generated files.
- “At most twenty posts per page” and “post order is preserved”:
  production-build test parses every archive page, counts rendered post links,
  asserts the count is no greater than twenty, asserts newest-first order within
  each page, and asserts the concatenated pages contain each post once in the
  original archive order.
- “Accessible previous/next navigation”:
  production-build test checks the rendered archive navigation landmark,
  accessible label, visible Previous/Next links, `rel` values, destination
  paths, and omission of the unavailable link at the first and last page.
  Human review should also confirm the labels are understandable when read
  without surrounding visual context.
- “Preserve home, tags, feed, sitemap, and individual-post navigation”:
  the same real build asserts the existing home selection/order, tag output and
  URLs, feed entry order, sitemap URLs, post routes/content, and any existing
  post-navigation links remain unchanged; archive pagination markup must not
  appear on individual post pages.
- “Static zero-JavaScript output”:
  the generated public HTML/XML is searched for script elements or injected
  runtime navigation code, and the archive links are verified as ordinary
  generated anchors.
- “Documentation is current”:
  inspect `docs/development/index.md` after the implementation and confirm its
  URL, limit, accessibility, and static-output claims match the generated
  files and passing integration test.

### Additional implementation verification

- Run `npm test` and the production `npm run build` from a clean working tree
  state appropriate to the repository.
- Inspect the generated output for trailing-slash URL consistency and ensure
  no empty archive page is emitted when the post count is an exact multiple of
  twenty.
- Confirm the temporary large-post fixture is isolated and cleaned up so test
  data cannot become public content or leave unrelated repository changes.

# Add optional pagination to the notes collection

Plan the addition of optional `limit`/`offset` pagination to `GET /notes/`
while preserving its current JSON-array response when pagination is not
requested. This task is planning-only; implementation is not authorized by
this handoff.

## Requirements checklist

- [ ] `GET /notes/` accepts optional `limit` and `offset` query parameters.
- [ ] A paginated request returns a bounded JSON-array slice in ascending
  note-ID order, with `offset` applied before `limit`.
- [ ] A paginated response exposes the total number of notes in a response
  header.
- [ ] A request with neither pagination parameter retains the current
  full-list JSON-array behavior.
- [ ] Invalid pagination values are rejected through normal FastAPI request
  validation.
- [ ] The other note CRUD routes retain their current behavior.
- [ ] Public API documentation describes the supported pagination behavior
  after the contract is finalized and implemented.

## Unresolved requirement questions

- What exact response-header name should carry the total count? The
  implementation plan recommends `X-Total-Count`, but this is a public API
  contract and needs confirmation.
- Should the total-count header be emitted only when `limit` or `offset` is
  supplied, or on the unpaginated full-list response as well? The current
  reading is paginated responses only.
- What numeric bounds are required? The recommended baseline is
  `offset >= 0` and `limit >= 1` when supplied, using FastAPI's declared
  parameter constraints so malformed and out-of-range values produce the
  framework's ordinary `422` validation response. A maximum page size has not
  been requested.

## Research and supporting facts

- `src/app/api/notes.py` currently exposes `GET /` under the `/notes` router
  and returns `await crud.get_all()` directly.
- `src/app/api/crud.py` currently has only an unbounded `get_all()` query.
- `src/app/db.py` stores notes in a table with an integer primary-key `id`.
- `src/tests/test_notes.py` has a basic collection-response check and only a
  minimal CRUD-route smoke check; it has no pagination, ordering, validation,
  header, or non-regression coverage.
- `README.md` currently states that the collection route returns every note as
  a JSON array. No notes-query specification exists under `docs/`.

## Execution plan

Status: Draft

The collection endpoint should remain an array-returning route. The route
should declare optional integer query parameters through FastAPI, allowing
FastAPI to own parsing and constraint errors. It should distinguish the
no-parameter path from the paginated path so existing full-list behavior stays
compatible.

For the paginated path, the data-access layer should query notes ordered by
ascending primary-key ID, apply the offset, and then apply the limit when
present. It should obtain the total count from the notes table independently
of the page slice. The route should attach that count to the response using
the confirmed header name. Existing read-one, create, update, and delete
handlers and their data-access operations should remain unchanged.

Verification should cross the public HTTP boundary using the real FastAPI
route, database, and test application. Seed a known set of notes through the
public API, then verify:

- an ordinary `GET /notes/` remains a JSON array containing the full set;
- a request with both parameters returns the expected ascending-ID slice and
  total-count header;
- requests with only `limit` or only `offset` have the defined semantics;
- an empty or beyond-end slice still reports the full total;
- malformed and out-of-range values receive FastAPI's normal `422`
  validation response;
- the existing detail, create, update, and delete paths still work through
  their public endpoints.

The maintained `README.md` should be updated in the same implementation
change with the final parameter bounds, slice semantics, and header name. No
new documentation directory or placeholder specification is needed.

### Implementation decisions and open questions

- Keep the response shape as a JSON array; do not introduce a pagination
  envelope.
- Make ascending `id` ordering explicit for paginated queries so page
  membership is deterministic.
- Preserve the existing unpaginated code path as far as practical, rather
  than changing the behavior of unrelated CRUD operations.
- Resolve the header name, header emission scope, and exact parameter bounds
  before changing the status from Draft to Approved.

### Documentation

- Update `README.md` after the public contract is resolved and implemented.
- Document that omitting both parameters preserves the full-list array.
- Document the query parameters, ascending-ID ordering, total-count header,
  and validation behavior.
- Do not present the target behavior as current documentation while this task
  remains unimplemented.

### Task checklist

- [ ] Confirm the unresolved public-contract questions.
- [ ] Change the task status to `Approved` after the contract is confirmed.
- [ ] Add optional FastAPI-validated pagination parameters to the collection
  route.
- [ ] Add ordered, offset/limit page retrieval and total-count retrieval.
- [ ] Attach the confirmed total-count header on the defined responses.
- [ ] Add public integration coverage for paginated and unpaginated behavior,
  validation, ordering, empty pages, and header contents.
- [ ] Add public non-regression coverage for the other CRUD routes as needed.
- [ ] Update `README.md` with the implemented contract.
- [ ] Run the focused test suite and record the result.

### Requirement verification

- Optional parameters and normal invalid-input handling: public
  `GET /notes/` requests with omitted, malformed, and out-of-range query
  values; verify the successful array response and FastAPI `422` boundary.
- Bounded ascending-ID slices and total count: public seeded requests with
  both parameters, single parameters, and an empty/beyond-end page; verify
  item IDs, page length, and the confirmed response header against the seeded
  total.
- Full-list compatibility: public request without either parameter; verify
  the response remains a JSON array containing all seeded notes.
- CRUD compatibility: public create, detail, update, and delete requests
  using the existing API paths; verify their current status and payload
  behavior.
- Documentation: inspect the final README claims against the implemented
  route contract after tests pass.

### Additional implementation verification

- Run the existing test suite to catch regressions outside the new focused
  cases.
- Inspect the generated FastAPI route schema after implementation to ensure
  the optional parameters and validation constraints are exposed as intended.
